name: Lena Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the assistant organist at St Columba's, the big church on Chapel Hill, so I play for weekday Masses, choir practice and a lot of funerals and weddings. Between services I teach piano to eight children in the front room of our flat, mostly scales and hymn tunes to start. Father Tom (the parish priest) calls me when a family books a funeral, and I sit with them to choose the hymns, which is the part I find most meaningful. I'm still learning; Mr Doyle, the head organist, plays the big Sunday services because my pedal work isn't good enough yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things for you money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Very steady, thank God. Funerals and weddings pay a proper fee, and the parish pays me a salary for the weekday work. My parents helped Mateo (my fiancé) and me buy our flat, so we've only a small mortgage, and I've about ten months of money saved besides. I don't use any of the AI things. I don't really see why I'd need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people got carried away, as they do with every new gadget. Music in church has been played by people for a thousand years, and that won't change for an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, though it wouldn't surprise me. What does worry me is fewer people coming to church, which means fewer weddings over time. That's been happening slowly since before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, with the parish work and my eight pupils. I'd keep up my organ lessons with Mr Doyle so I can take some Sundays. Mateo and I would get married next June as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. That's the life I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer people come to church. How does that show up in your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There were thirty-one weddings at my church, St Columba's, when I started and nineteen this year. Funerals stay steady, sadly. If it keeps falling, my fee income drops, even without any computers involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in your work get automated here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the parish office would use a computer for the booking diary. Mrs Kelly (the parish secretary) would grumble about that. The music itself would stay with us.

say: People **got carried away**, as they do with every new gadget.
Church music has been played by **real people** for a thousand years.
think: **Fewer people** coming to church is my real worry.
Falling **wedding numbers** cut my fees, with or without computers.
do: Carry on with **parish work** and eight piano pupils.
Keep up **organ lessons** with Mr Doyle to take some Sundays.
feel: **Peaceful**, because it's the life she wants.

fieldNote: Her real pressure is **falling church attendance**, which predates AI.
She has **family help** and a small mortgage behind her.
Her **faith** shapes both her work and her sense of what lasts.

steps.text: Carry on with parish organ work and eight piano pupils
Keep up organ lessons with Mr Doyle to play some Sundays
Marry Mateo next June as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some things shouldn't be handed to a computer, and worship is one of them. I'd say that to anyone at the parish who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my piano pupils are more at risk than the church work. Parents are busy and there'll be apps that teach a child for less than I charge. Some small parishes in the countryside already use a hymn player instead of an organist. That could spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my prices for pupils the same and make sure the parents see their children improving, with little concerts at Christmas. I'd ask Father Tom whether the diocese is planning anything with recorded music. I wouldn't learn the apps; I'd rather be better at what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. But I trust things will be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if lessons dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the parents, really. It's the big tech firms selling cheap everything, and people who've got used to wanting things for nothing. Good things cost something, and I think people will learn that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the government have a part to play?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather it didn't. Families and the parish look after their own. If I lost pupils, Mateo and my parents would help, and I'd find more funerals and weddings in other parishes.

fieldNote: She blames **big tech** and cheap habits, not the parents.

Her main income looks **safe** to her, though pupils may drift away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to hold on to what makes us human: family, faith, music played by real hands. I'd say it at the parish and to family, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the teaching is gone by 2028. Then robots in 2031 could play an organ well enough, I suppose. I'd hope the church keeps a person, but bishops have budgets too, and I'd only be the assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Doyle to teach me twice a week so I'm good enough to be kept on when the cuts come. I'd look for funeral work in more parishes now, while families still want a person. And Mateo and I would still marry next June, but we'd put off trying for a baby for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. More than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the years when the church still needs my hands. I'd want to be properly good by then, and known by every funeral director in the town. That's how you're kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather the government stayed out. Does that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, I don't know. If whole towns lose their work at once, families can't carry everyone. But I'd still want work, not a cheque in the post.

I'd say that at the **parish**, not online.

do: Take organ lessons with Mr Doyle **twice a week**.

**Delay a baby** by a year or two after the wedding.
feel: **Anxious**, more than she'd say out loud.
S2.quote: If whole towns lose their work at once, families can't carry everyone. But I'd still want work, not a cheque in the post.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her **teaching income** but hopes the church keeps her.
Her views **soften** slightly on government help when whole towns are hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families and parishes to prepare, and that we should look after each other. I'd say that after Mass if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years would let me become good enough to share the Sunday services with Mr Doyle. He's 63 and wants to step back. If I'm the parish organist by 2031, I think the church keeps me longer than an assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise on the big organ every evening after choir. I'd keep my pupils as long as they come, without changing how I teach. We'd marry next June and start a family soon after, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd have a purpose. It's something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the parish decides to use a machine anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look for a parish that hasn't. Not every priest will want a robot at a funeral. I'd follow the work, even to another town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mateo say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo (my fiancé) is a carpenter, so his work's safe longer than mine. He'd say we'd manage, and we would. His family have a workshop we could always lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and good things like church music last. I'd tell people not to fret.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel quite safe. By 2036 I'd hope to be the parish organist with children of my own. Robots in 2039 feel like another lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd practise, keep my pupils, and get married. I'd see what other parishes do before changing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots feel like another lifetime. Would you plan for them at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I'll be honest. I'd save as I always do. Maybe around 2034 I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to learn a trade with their hands, like my fiancé Mateo, and music for the love of it. I wouldn't want them depending on a computer for their living.

I'd tell people at St Columba's **not to fret** about it.

S4.quote: I'd want my children to learn a trade with their hands, like my fiancé Mateo, and music for the love of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only be the assistant organist when the cuts came, and I'd have lost my pupils too. What would help is the church deciding, firmly, that worship stays with people, and parishes sharing work between them so musicians aren't left out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a funeral is like without a real person playing. I've seen a funeral with a speaker, and the family kept looking at the box on the table, waiting for something. It was very sad.
